hero.basedOn: A model estimate, not a direct count. 1,933 US adults with Android phones let an app log their use for 12 weeks in spring 2020; some got pay or app locks at random. The model put self-control problems at 31% of their use.
hero.caveat: 'Social media' here means six app types, including web browsers and YouTube. Volunteers at the start of the pandemic. The 31% rests on the model; a more cautious reading of the same data gives 16%.
hero.numberCheck: 31% matches the fetched text: 48 minutes per day, 31 percent of baseline use (primary model). Analysis sample 1,933 (balanced panel). Authors' conservative estimate without habit formation = the limit effect, 22 min/day (16 percent); alternative assumptions mostly larger. Covers six app types (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, browsers, YouTube).

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).
ref.quote: our primary model prediction is that eliminating self-control problems would reduce FITSBY use by 48 minutes per day, or 31 percent of baseline use

stats.line: Students' own iPhone logs showed about 6 hours 53 minutes of phone use a day and 113 pickups a day.
stats.mirror: You pick up your phone over a hundred times a day.

basis.who: undergraduate students with iPhones, mean age 20.1; 18% men
basis.n: 187 students (34 of them men)
basis.measured: Weekly screenshots of the iPhone 'Screen Time' page: hours of use and number of pickups, logged by the phone, not guessed.

stats.caveat: Mostly women, during a pandemic semester. The same study found a week of heavier use did not predict a worse mood that week.

ref.cite: Bradley AHM, Howard AL (2023). Stress and mood associations with smartphone use in university students: a 12-week longitudinal study. Clinical Psychological Science 11(5):921-941.
ref.quote: On average, students used their smartphones for 6 hr 53 min per day and picked up their phones 113 times.

stats.line: 84% of male Norwegian students use a screen in bed; people who do spend about 42 minutes a night on it.
stats.mirror: You use your phone in bed almost every night.

basis.who: full-time college and university students aged 18 to 28; this figure is the men
basis.n: 15,097 male students (of 45,654 in the study)
basis.measured: Any screen use after going to bed, self-reported. The 42 minutes is the nightly average among all 39,809 students who use screens in bed, men and women; they did it about 6 nights a week.

stats.caveat: Self-report; people misjudge screen time. Students only. Women did it a little more often (89%).

ref.cite: Hjetland GJ, Skogen JC, Hysing M, Gradisar M, Sivertsen B (2025). How and when screens are used: comparing different screen activities and sleep in Norwegian university students. Frontiers in Psychiatry 16:1548273.

stats.line: About 6 in 10 Americans aged 18 to 29 say they are online almost constantly.
stats.mirror: You are online almost all day, like most people your age.

basis.who: US adults, weighted to match the population
basis.n: 546 adults aged 18 to 29 (of 5,733 surveyed)
basis.measured: Share who answered that they use the internet 'almost constantly'. Self-report. All adults: 41%; ages 18-29: 62%.

stats.caveat: 'Online' means anything: music, messages, work, not only social media. People judge this themselves, so it is a feeling, not a measured time.

ref.cite: Gelles-Watnick R (2024). Americans' use of mobile technology and home broadband. Pew Research Center, 31 January 2024.
ref.quote: About six-in-ten adults ages 18 to 29 (62%) say they are constantly online

basis.measured: Share scoring above a cut-off on a questionnaire. Strict rules: 5%; 'severe' cut-off: 13%; 'moderate' cut-off: 25%.

stats.caveat: A questionnaire score is not a diagnosis. Rates were twice as high in collectivist nations (31%) as in individualist ones (14%).

ref.cite: Cheng C, Lau YC, Chan L, Luk JW (2021). Prevalence of social media addiction across 32 nations: meta-analysis with subgroup analysis of classification schemes and cultural values. Addictive Behaviors 117:106845.
ref.quote: The pooled prevalence estimate was 5% (95% CI: 3%-7%) for studies adopting monothetic or strict monothetic classifications.

stats.line: Paid to cut social media for three weeks, people still used 19 minutes a day less three weeks after the pay stopped.
stats.mirror: You scroll today mostly because you scrolled yesterday.

basis.who: US adults with Android phones, recruited via Facebook and Instagram ads
basis.n: 1,933 adults who finished the study; about 1 in 4 got the pay offer
basis.when: March to July 2020 (start of the pandemic)
basis.measured: App-logged daily minutes on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, web browsers and YouTube. Pay cut use by 56 minutes a day; the effect shrank to 12 minutes a day after six weeks.

stats.caveat: This shows the habit itself: less use now means less use later, and more use builds more use. Volunteers, not representative.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).

stats.line: In 2020, 37% of US parents of 9- to 11-year-olds said their child already had their own smartphone.

basis.measured: Parents' answer to whether their child aged 9 to 11 has their own smartphone. Most of those children got it between ages 9 and 11.

ref.cite: Pew Research Center (2020). Children's engagement with digital devices, screen time. In: Parenting children in the age of screens, 28 July 2020.

stats.line: Each extra hour on a screen in bed went with 24 minutes less sleep and 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms.
stats.mirror: You wake up tired after one more video in bed.

basis.n: 39,809 students who use a screen in bed (of 45,654)

stats.caveat: One snapshot in time: poor sleepers may also reach for the phone more. Odds, not risk. Self-reported.

ref.cite: Hjetland GJ, Skogen JC, Hysing M, Gradisar M, Sivertsen B (2025). How and when screens are used: comparing different screen activities and sleep in Norwegian university students. Frontiers in Psychiatry 16:1548273.

stats.line: 52% of Americans aged 18 to 29 in a relationship say their partner is at least sometimes distracted by their phone.
stats.mirror: You look at your phone while she is talking to you.

basis.who: US adults; this figure is partnered adults aged 18-29
basis.n: 2,850 adults in a relationship whose partner has a phone (of 4,860 surveyed); Pew didn't report how many were aged 18 to 29
basis.measured: Share of married, cohabiting or committed adults who say their partner is often or sometimes distracted by their phone while they try to talk.

stats.caveat: This is how the partner sees it, not a measured cost. 2019 data; the share was higher (62%) among those aged 30-49.

ref.cite: Vogels EA, Anderson M (2020). Dating and relationships in the digital age. Pew Research Center, 8 May 2020.

stats.line: Adults in a social media trial said they spent about 8 hours a week on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter and TikTok.
stats.mirror: You say you have no time to train or read.

basis.who: adults recruited via social media, mean age 29.6; 62% women
basis.n: 154 adults
basis.measured: Self-reported minutes per week on four apps before the trial began. The group that kept scrolling logged 580 minutes a week by app at follow-up.

stats.caveat: Self-reported, and people misjudge their own screen time. Only four apps counted; YouTube and messaging not included.

ref.cite: Lambert J, Barnstable G, Minter E, Cooper J, McEwan D (2022). Taking a one-week break from social media improves well-being, depression, and anxiety: a randomized controlled trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 25(5):287-293.
ref.quote: At baseline, participants self-reported spending a mean of more than 484 minutes per week on SM

stats.mirror: You fear a day without your phone would be unbearable.

basis.who: university students, mean age 22.4; 33% men
basis.n: 36 students who did all four sessions (45 started)
basis.measured: Questionnaires on mood, anxiety and craving, before, during and after 24 hours with the phone sealed in a bag.

stats.caveat: Small, one day only, students. Craving was already high just before the phone was handed in, and fell once it came back.

ref.cite: Wilcockson TDW, Osborne AM, Ellis DA (2019). Digital detox: the effect of smartphone abstinence on mood, anxiety, and craving. Addictive Behaviors 99:106013.
ref.quote: we measured three variables (mood, anxiety, and craving) on four occasions, which included a 24-hour period of smartphone abstinence

stats.line: Switching the phone to black-and-white (greyscale) cut screen time by about 28 minutes a day.
stats.mirror: You open apps without knowing why.

basis.design: crossover trial, one week each; order set by sign-up date, not by chance
basis.who: first-year medical students
basis.n: 51 students who finished both weeks (61 started)
basis.where: USA (California University of Science and Medicine, Colton, California)
basis.measured: Daily screen time from the phone's built-in tracker, one week greyscale versus one week colour.

stats.caveat: Small and short. A larger trial (112 people) also found greyscale cut logged screen time quickly, but saw no change in well-being.

ref.cite: Hagerty J, Saretha S, Phung B, et al. (2026). A cross-over feasibility trial of smartphone grayscale mode in medical students. Frontiers in Digital Health 8:1816095.
ref.quote: Grayscale mode was associated with a statistically significant reduction in mean daily screen time compared to color display (mean reduction 28 min per day; p < 0.05).

stats.line: No phone in the last 30 minutes before bed: people fell asleep about 12 minutes faster and slept about 18 minutes longer.
stats.mirror: You scroll in bed and then can't switch off.

basis.who: university students with poor sleep and a bedtime phone habit
basis.n: 38 students (19 asked to stop, 19 not)
basis.measured: Sleep diary (time to fall asleep, sleep length), a sleep-quality questionnaire, mood and a memory task.

stats.caveat: Tiny trial, self-reported sleep. It tested no phone before bed, not phone out of the bedroom.

ref.cite: He JW, Tu ZH, Xiao L, Su T, Tang YX (2020). Effect of restricting bedtime mobile phone use on sleep, arousal, mood, and working memory: a randomized pilot trial. PLoS ONE 15(2):e0228756.
ref.quote: Sleep latency in the intervention group was reduced by around 12 minutes and sleep duration was increased by around 18 minutes.

stats.line: After one week off social media, people felt better and less depressed and anxious than those who kept scrolling.
stats.mirror: You wonder if a short break would make any difference.

basis.who: adults recruited via social media, mean age 29.6; 62% women
basis.n: 154 adults
basis.measured: Well-being, depression and anxiety questionnaires. Use fell from about 510 to 21 self-reported minutes a week (app-logged: 28 vs 580 in the control group).

stats.caveat: Short trial, mostly young women, and people knew their group. Pooled reviews of break trials disagree on whether mood really improves.

ref.cite: Lambert J, Barnstable G, Minter E, Cooper J, McEwan D (2022). Taking a one-week break from social media improves well-being, depression, and anxiety: a randomized controlled trial. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 25(5):287-293.
ref.quote: At a 1-week follow-up, significant between-group differences in well-being (mean difference [MD] 4.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.0-6.8), depression (MD -2.2

stats.line: Four weeks off Facebook freed about an hour a day and made people a bit happier; 80% said the break was good for them.
stats.mirror: You want your evenings back.

basis.who: US adult Facebook users who used it more than 15 minutes a day
basis.n: 1,661 adults (580 paid to switch Facebook off, 1,081 kept using it)
basis.when: Oct-Nov 2018, four weeks before the midterm election
basis.measured: Survey index of happiness, life satisfaction, depression and anxiety (up 0.09 SD). Weeks later, the break group's Facebook app use was still 22% lower.

stats.caveat: The mood gain was small. Participants were younger, more educated and more left-leaning than average users, and were paid.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The welfare effects of social media. American Economic Review 110(3):629-676 (working paper version of 8 Nov 2019).
ref.quote: Facebook deactivation increased subjective well-being, and 80 percent of the Treatment group reported that deactivation was good for them.

stats.line: Six weeks off Facebook made people a little happier and less down or anxious. Instagram breaks helped less.
stats.mirror: You expect one break to change everything at once.

basis.who: US Facebook and Instagram users who used the app at least 15 minutes a day
basis.n: 19,857 Facebook users and 15,585 Instagram users; 27% were offered pay for the six-week break, the rest for one week
basis.when: six weeks before the November 2020 election
basis.measured: Self-reported happiness, depression and anxiety, combined into one score. Controls also took a break, but for only one week.

stats.caveat: Small gain, mostly in people over 35; the Instagram gain was mostly in women under 25 and missed the study's own bar. Not yet reviewed by outside experts; several authors work at Meta.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Wittenbrink B, et al. (2025). The effect of deactivating Facebook and Instagram on users' emotional state. NBER Working Paper 33697.
ref.quote: People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety

stats.line: After four paid weeks off Facebook, only 1 in 20 people still had it switched off nine weeks later. Most came back, but by their own count used the app about 12 minutes a day less than people who had kept using it.
stats.mirror: You quit once, went back, and think the break was wasted.

basis.who: US adult Facebook users who used it more than 15 minutes a day, paid to switch it off
basis.n: 580 people paid to switch Facebook off for four weeks (of 1,661 in the trial)
basis.when: Oct-Nov 2018; checked up to nine weeks after the break
basis.measured: Whether each account was still switched off, checked about once a day after the break: 11% a week later and 5% nine weeks later, against 3% and 2.5% of the comparison group. A month on, they also said they used the Facebook app 12 minutes a day less (23%).

stats.caveat: Ordinary users, not people with a problem, and paid to switch it off, not delete it, so a free choice may stick differently. The 12 minutes are people's own estimates; among iPhone users who read their phone's tracker, the drop was less than half as big and could be chance.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Braghieri L, Eichmeyer S, Gentzkow M (2020). The welfare effects of social media. American Economic Review 110(3):629-676 (working paper version of 8 Nov 2019).
ref.quote: five percent of the Treatment group still had their accounts deactivated nine weeks after the experiment ended

stats.line: Of 134 German teenagers who scored as problem internet users on a questionnaire, 96 (about 7 in 10) were below the problem line a year later, with no treatment at all.
stats.mirror: You think a habit this strong never fades without help.

basis.design: one-year follow-up of the untreated comparison group in a school prevention trial
basis.who: school pupils, average age 15, who scored at the problem level on a compulsive internet use questionnaire; none were in treatment
basis.n: 134 pupils with problem-level scores (96 below the line a year later)
basis.where: Germany (34 schools in Baden-Württemberg, Hesse and Rhineland-Palatinate)
basis.measured: Compulsive Internet Use Scale score at the start and 12 months later; 24 points or more counted as problem use.

stats.caveat: Teenagers, and internet use in general, games included. The questionnaire gave shaky readings at the start, and scores just over a line often drift back down by chance. Boys got out more often than girls; 3 in 10 were still stuck a year on.

ref.cite: Wartberg L, Lindenberg K (2020). Predictors of spontaneous remission of problematic internet use in adolescence: a one-year follow-up study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17:448.
ref.quote: The subjects who had a CIUS sum value of <24 at t2 (n = 96) were assigned to the group with spontaneous remission of problematic Internet use.

stats.line: Of 152 adults who agreed to stay off social media for a week, 59% slipped at least once.
stats.mirror: You slipped back onto the apps within days and think you failed.

basis.design: one-week study with phone check-ins three times a day; no comparison group
basis.who: adults aged 18 to 80 who agreed to a week off social media; about 70% women
basis.n: 152 adults
basis.where: German-speaking Europe (research team in Krems and Vienna, Austria, and Konstanz, Germany)
basis.measured: Craving, boredom and mood three times a day; each evening, whether and how long they had used social media. 4 days as usual, 7 days off, 4 days after.

stats.caveat: Mostly women who chose to try, not people with a problem, and WhatsApp counted as social media. The slips were small: on average fewer than two, of about three minutes each, says the university's news release. Craving and boredom rose during the week; use did not shoot up after it.

ref.cite: Stieger S, Lewetz D (2018). A week without using social media: results from an ecological momentary intervention study using smartphones. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 21:618-624.
ref.quote: a substantial number of participants (59 percent) relapsed at least once during the intervention phase

stats.line: In 2018, about 4 in 10 US Facebook users had taken a break of several weeks in the past year, and 1 in 4 had deleted the app from their phone.
stats.mirror: You've thought about deleting the app but feel it's an extreme step.

basis.design: national survey (Pew Research Center's American Trends Panel)
basis.who: US adults who use Facebook
basis.n: 3,413 Facebook users (of 4,594 adults surveyed)
basis.measured: In the past 12 months: took a break from checking Facebook for several weeks or more (42%); deleted the app from their phone (26%, and 44% of users aged 18 to 29).

stats.caveat: Asked just after a big privacy scandal, and it did not ask why, so many breaks may have been about privacy, not habit. It does not say how many stayed off or put the app back.

ref.cite: Perrin A (2018). Americans are changing their relationship with Facebook. Pew Research Center, 5 September 2018.
ref.quote: Around four-in-ten (42%) say they have taken a break from checking the platform for a period of several weeks or more

stats.line: About 4 in 10 young adults in Austria (41.7%) used an app such as Screen Time to watch or limit their phone use.
stats.mirror: You've set screen-time limits and still wonder if they do anything.

basis.design: online survey at one point in time
basis.who: young adults aged 18 to 35 (average 22) living in Austria, mostly students reached through a university network; 42% men
basis.n: 500 young adults
basis.measured: Use of apps that track or limit phone time; social media use, problem phone use and well-being.

stats.caveat: One snapshot of mostly students, not people with a problem; women used the apps more often. Among app users, more social media use did not go with more problem phone use, but that does not prove the apps did it. Having an app is not the same as sticking to its limits.

ref.cite: Schmuck D (2020). Does digital detox work? Exploring the role of digital detox applications for problematic smartphone use and well-being of young adults using multigroup analysis. Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking 23:526-532.
ref.quote: Results revealed that a high proportion of young adults use digital detox apps (41.7 percent).

stats.line: App locks people set for themselves cut their time on social media, browsers and YouTube by 22 minutes a day (16%), and 78% were still using them in the final weeks.
stats.mirror: You keep promising yourself you'll use it less tomorrow.

basis.who: US adults aged 18 to 64 with Android phones, recruited via Facebook and Instagram ads that did not mention phone use; 39% men
basis.n: 1,933 adults who finished the study; about 6 in 10 were offered the locks
basis.when: March to July 2020, 12 weeks of limits
basis.measured: App-logged minutes on Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, browsers and YouTube. Limits locked the app and could not be skipped at once.

stats.caveat: Ordinary users, not people with a problem, early in the pandemic, when most said their phone use was up. Phone-maker limits are easier to override, so may work less. The effect faded slightly, and people without locks underestimated their next weeks' use by about 6 minutes a day.

ref.cite: Allcott H, Gentzkow M, Song L (2022). Digital addiction. American Economic Review 112(7):2424-2463 (NBER Working Paper 28936, revised March 2022).
ref.quote: The limit treatment reduced FITSBY screen time by 22 minutes per day (16 percent) over 12 weeks.

stats.line: Cutting phone use by 1 hour a day for a week helped as much as or more than a week with no phone at all, and most gains lasted better over four months.
stats.mirror: You think it's all or nothing: delete everything or change nothing.

basis.who: adult smartphone users in Germany
basis.n: 619 adults: 200 went a week without the phone, 226 cut 1 hour a day, 193 changed nothing
basis.measured: Phone time, problem phone use, life satisfaction, low mood, anxiety, exercise and cigarettes, by online survey. Four months on, the cut-down group used the phone about 45 minutes a day less than before, the no-phone group 38 minutes less (university news release).

stats.caveat: Ordinary phone users, not people with a problem, and phone time was self-reported. The full week off helped too, just less lastingly; only the cut-down group also smoked fewer cigarettes.

ref.cite: Brailovskaia J, Delveaux J, John J, Wicker V, Noveski A, Kim S, Schillack H, Margraf J (2023). Finding the "sweet spot" of smartphone use: reduction or abstinence to increase well-being and healthy lifestyle?! An experimental intervention study. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 29:149-161.
ref.quote: Most effects were stronger and remained more stable over 4 months in the reduction group than in the abstinence group.

stats.line: Students who capped Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat at 10 minutes each a day felt less lonely and less depressed after three weeks than students who carried on as usual.
stats.mirror: You want to cut down, not delete everything.

basis.who: undergraduate students at the University of Pennsylvania
basis.n: 143 students
basis.measured: Loneliness and depression questionnaires, limited group versus use as usual. About 30 minutes a day in total across the three apps.

stats.caveat: Small, one university, three weeks, ordinary students. Both groups also felt less anxious, maybe just from tracking their own use.

ref.cite: Hunt MG, Marx R, Lipson C, Young J (2018). No more FOMO: limiting social media decreases loneliness and depression. Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology 37(10):751-768.
ref.quote: Our findings strongly suggest that limiting social media use to approximately 30 minutes per day may lead to significant improvement in well-being.

stats.line: Across 10 trials, using social media less eased low mood a little. Cutting down showed a clear effect; stopping outright (3 trials) did not, but that gap could be chance.
stats.mirror: You assume only quitting outright would lift your mood.

basis.who: mostly young adults (average age 24; 75% women)
basis.n: 1,491 people in 10 trials (7 of cutting down, 3 of stopping outright)
basis.when: published 2025; no trial lasted longer than 3 weeks
basis.measured: Depression symptoms after limiting or stopping social media, against carrying on as usual. Small effect (g = 0.25 after allowing for unpublished studies; 0.33 for cutting down alone).

stats.caveat: None of the trials picked people with a problem. Mostly young women, short trials, and only three checked again later. A slight lift, not a cure.

ref.cite: May W, Malouff JM, Meynadier J (2025). Reducing social media use decreases depression symptoms: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education 15:222.
ref.quote: reducing social media use significantly decreases depressive symptoms, with an effect size of g = 0.25, 95% CI [0.10, 0.41], p < 0.001, after adjusting for publication bias

stats.line: Ten studies with 4,674 people found that a full break from social media did not, on average, lift mood or life satisfaction.
stats.mirror: You're counting on a week off the apps to fix your mood.

basis.who: adults, often students; about 65% women
basis.n: 4,674 people in 10 studies
basis.when: published 2025; breaks of 1 to 28 days, most often 7
basis.measured: Good mood, bad mood and life satisfaction after a full break from social media, against carrying on. Break length made no clear difference.

stats.caveat: Ordinary users, not people with a problem; over half came from one US study of a month off Facebook. Short breaks and mixed methods. Counting only studies with a separate comparison group, good mood rose slightly. It measured mood, not time won back or sleep.

ref.cite: Lemahieu L, Vander Zwalmen Y, Mennes M, Koster EHW, Vanden Abeele MMP, Poels K (2025). The effects of social media abstinence on affective well-being and life satisfaction: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Scientific Reports 15:7581.
ref.quote: The analyses revealed no significant effects of social media abstinence interventions on positive affect, negative affect, or life satisfaction.

stats.line: In 20 trials of cutting down or stopping social media, efforts shorter than a week left people feeling slightly worse; a week or longer helped a little.
stats.mirror: You quit for two days, felt worse, and gave up.

basis.design: reanalysis of a meta-analysis of experiments
basis.who: people in trials of cutting down or stopping social media
basis.n: 20 trials (4 shorter than a week, 16 a week or longer); the reanalysis does not add up how many people
basis.measured: Mental-health scores after the break, against carrying on. Under a week: d = −0.18 (worse); a week or more: d = 0.16 (better). Around 3 weeks looked best.

stats.caveat: Both effects are small. All 20 trials together showed no clear effect, and the 3-week sweet spot still needs testing. A separate pooling of 10 studies found no link with break length.

ref.cite: Thrul J, Devkota J, AlJuboori D, Regan T, Alomairah S, Vidal C (2025). Social media reduction or abstinence interventions are providing mental health benefits: reanalysis of a published meta-analysis. Psychology of Popular Media 14:207-209.
ref.quote: interventions of <1 week resulted in significantly worse mental health outcomes (d = −0.175), while interventions of 1 week or longer resulted in significant improvements (d = 0.156)

rejected.claim: Ofcom Online Nation 2025: UK 18-24s online about 6 h 20 min a day (passive measurement)
rejected.why: Ofcom site blocked every fetch (403 / bot check); figure seen only in secondary news reports. Not used.

rejected.claim: Sapien Labs (Thiagarajan 2025): smartphone before age 13 linked to worse young-adult mind health, n > 100,000
rejected.why: Its headline numbers are about suicidal thoughts (crisis content), it is correlational with recalled age, and authors fund the data. Not fetched in full.

rejected.claim: Phone out of the bedroom improves sleep (trial)
rejected.why: No trial found that tested removing the phone from the bedroom. Used the 'no phone 30 minutes before bed' pilot instead.

rejected.claim: Zimmermann & Sobolev 2023 greyscale trial (n=112): size of screen-time drop
rejected.why: Abstract gives no number; used only in the greyscale caveat (drop in logged time, no well-being change).

rejected.claim: Brailovskaia 2022 (n=619, Germany): 1 hour less a day for a week beat full abstinence, effects held 4 months
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out, but left out to stay within 14 new stats; the only number is the 1-hour dose. Good backup.

rejected.claim: Pew 2024: 38% of US teens say they spend too much time on their phone; 47% of parents say the same of themselves
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out (n=1,453 teens and parents, Sept-Oct 2023). Left out: teens and parents, not the reader's age. Backup.

rejected.claim: Pew 2024: nearly half of US teens online almost constantly, up from 24% a decade ago (n=1,391)
rejected.why: Fetched and checks out; left out to keep the 'start' group to two items. Backup.

rejected.claim: Hero quote 'self-control problems drive 31% of social media use'
rejected.why: Not wrong, but loose: the paper's 31% covers six app types including web browsers and YouTube, and it is a model output, not a count.

rejected.claim: Short CBT group therapy freed 69% of men with internet addiction, against 24% on a waiting list (Wölfling 2019, JAMA Psychiatry, 143 men).
rejected.why: Fetched (PMID 31290948, full text): men only and a strong trial, but the main problems were online games (57%), porn (16%) and general internet use; social media was not counted on its own. Better fit for a gaming or porn page.

rejected.claim: 99 Days of Freedom: people who felt addicted to Facebook were more likely to go back early (Baumer 2015, Social Media + Society, 5,000+ surveys).
